46009-the-privy-purse-expenses-of-king-h:
The Privy Purse Expenses of King Henry the Eighth is an edition of the king's household accounts. Nicolas edited it from the original manuscript with notes. The accounts run from November 1529 to December 1532. A publisher's notice praises the volume's curious particulars. They illustrate the manners, customs, and expenses of the time. They also show the personal character of Henry himself, it says. From the accounts the king's place on each day can be traced. His occupations and amusements appear day by day.

The names and wages of his household are recorded in them. Sums paid for jewels, books, furniture, and clothes are entered. The charges of the king's fools and jester are included. Expenses of his meeting with the French king at Calais appear. Numerous entries relative to Anne Boleyn are called new and important. Each month's account is examined and signed by the king.
60670-work-of-the-colored-law-and-order-:
Waring wrote this report of the Colored Law and Order League for the Committee of Twelve for the Advancement of the Negro Race, at Cheyney, Pennsylvania. The League's president was John Holmes, a minister; its work began in talk after the Atlanta riot. Colored Baltimoreans saw in their neighborhoods some of the causes of that horror. Their city had no incendiary press, the report grants, but it had sections infested with saloons.

A map makes the case. In the lower Druid Hill Avenue district there were forty-two saloons against fifteen churches and twelve schools. Among them stood a home for old people and the colored Young Men's and Young Women's Christian Associations. The saloons, kept by white men of the lowest type, had police protection, as testimony before the Liquor License Board showed. The League organized to shut the dens that schooled colored children in crime.
